Thanksgiving 2026 holiday travel across the United States is being strained by powerful storms on both coasts, lingering fallout from airline technology glitches and some of the heaviest passenger volumes in more than a decade, leading to long airport lines, regional flight delays and challenging driving conditions in several states.

## Record holiday demand collides with fragile airline operations

The Federal Aviation Administration forecast that U.S. skies would be busier over the 2026 Thanksgiving period than at any time in the past 16 years, with nearly 418,000 flights scheduled between November 23 and December 1. Airlines scheduled that capacity after several years of robust holiday travel and only a slight expected dip in the number of passengers compared with 2025, based on industry and federal projections released earlier in the week. At the same time, multiple recent technology disruptions have highlighted how sensitive day-of travel remains to even short interruptions.

On Sunday November 22, more than 1,000 Delta Air Lines flights were delayed after an automated system used to calculate aircraft weight and balance malfunctioned during one of the first major outbound days for Thanksgiving travelers. United Airlines also reported a separate system outage and briefly grounded its departures earlier in the month, according to company and FAA statements. While both carriers said the problems were resolved and no FAA air traffic systems were involved, the episodes created aircraft and crew dislocations that have taken several days to fully unwind, particularly at large hubs such as Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.
